entry: New Zealand [[Rugby union|rugby union]] player, a winger regarded as the first true global superstar of the sport. Born in Pukekohe to [[Tonga|Tongan]] immigrants, he grew up between rural Tonga and South [[Auckland]]. He excelled at athletics and rugby at Wesley College before pursuing a professional career. He became the youngest All Black when he debuted in 1994, aged 19 years and 45 days. He was acknowledged as the top player at the 1995 [[Rugby World Cup]], with a four-try performance in the semi-final against England. He shares the Rugby World Cup all-time try-scoring record of 15 with Bryan Habana, set in only two tournaments. He finished his international career with 63 caps and 37 tries. He was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome, a genetic kidney disorder, in 1995, and his illness forced his retirement from professional rugby in 2007. He died unexpectedly at home in Auckland.

American virologist and medical researcher. Born in [[New York City]], he attended the City College of New York and New York University School of Medicine. In 1947 he became a professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, where he worked to determine the number of poliovirus types. For the next seven years he devoted himself to developing a [[Polio vaccine|vaccine]] against polio. The vaccine's success was made public in April 1955, and Salk chose not to patent it. An immediate rush to vaccinate followed, and by 1959 the vaccine had reached about 90 countries. Less than 25 years after the release of Salk's vaccine, domestic polio transmission had been eliminated in the United States. In 1963 he founded the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, California. He campaigned for mandatory vaccination, calling universal vaccination of children a "moral commitment."

American revivalist preacher, philosopher and Congregationalist theologian. Scholars stress how central the [[Age of Enlightenment]] was to his thinking. He played a critical role in shaping the First Great Awakening and oversaw revivals in 1733–35 at his church in Northampton, Massachusetts. His work gave rise to [[New England]] theology. In 1741, at a revival in Enfield, Connecticut, he delivered the sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God," following a tour of the [[Thirteen Colonies]] by George Whitefield. His book *The Life of David Brainerd* inspired missionaries throughout the 19th century. Although many scientists were pushed toward [[Deism|deism]], he believed the natural world showed God's design. He was fascinated by the discoveries of [[Isaac Newton]]. He died from a smallpox inoculation shortly after becoming president of the [[Princeton University|College of New Jersey]] in Princeton.

American composer, lyricist and playwright. He is known for the musicals [[Rent (musical)|Rent]] and *Tick, Tick... Boom!*, which explored [[Multiculturalism|multiculturalism]], [[Substance use disorder|substance use disorder]] and homophobia. Larson died from an aortic dissection the day before the first preview of *Rent* off-Broadway. The show moved to Broadway, became one of the longest-running Broadway productions and was adapted into a 2005 film. Larson posthumously received three Tony Awards and the [[Pulitzer Prize]] for Drama.

Welsh actor. Known for stage, film and television work, Pryce won two Tony Awards, for *Comedians* (1977) and for the Broadway transfer of *Miss Saigon* (1991). He also won two Laurence Olivier Awards, including for the title role in [[Hamlet]] (1980). His breakthrough screen role was in [[Terry Gilliam]]'s *Brazil* (1985). He earned his first Academy Award nomination for playing [[Pope Francis]] in *The Two Popes* (2019). On television he played [[Thomas Wolsey]] in *Wolf Hall*, Prince Philip in *The Crown* and the High Sparrow in [[Game of Thrones]]. He was knighted in 2021 for services to drama.

English broadcaster and comedian. He presented *The Last Resort with Jonathan Ross* on Channel 4 in 1987–88 and later the [[BBC]] chat show *Friday Night with Jonathan Ross* (2001–2010), which won him three British Academy Television Awards. He hosted a BBC Radio 2 show from 1999 to 2010 and was film critic on the programme *Film…*. He was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire in 2005 for services to broadcasting. His semi-autobiographical book *Why Do I Say These Things?* was published in 2008.

Anglo-Irish writer, essayist, [[Satire|satirist]] and Anglican cleric. He wrote the satirical prose novel *Gulliver's Travels* (1726), which created the fictional island of Lilliput, and is regarded by many as the greatest satirist of the Georgian era. He originally published all of his works under pseudonyms, including Isaac Bickerstaff, or anonymously. *A Tale of a Tub* (1704) and *A Modest Proposal* (1729) display the deadpan, ironic style later termed Swiftian. He supported the [[Glorious Revolution]] and joined the Whigs early in his career. In 1700 he moved to Trim, County Meath, where many of his major works were written. In 1713 he was appointed dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in [[Dublin]]. He influenced later writers including John Ruskin and [[George Orwell]].

Commune in [[Guyana]] established by the Peoples Temple. On November 18, 1978, 918 people died in a coordinated mass murder-suicide across Jonestown, a nearby airstrip at Port Kaituma, and the group's headquarters in Georgetown. A total of 909 people died in Jonestown itself, all but two from apparent [[Cyanide|cyanide]] poisoning, and many were injected against their will. The poisonings followed the killing of five others, including U.S. Congressman Leo Ryan, at Port Kaituma, which [[Jim Jones]] had ordered. Early media accounts often called the deaths a mass suicide; later sources also use massacre or mass murder.

Canadian and American singer-songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and painter. Known for personal lyrics and unconventional compositions, she incorporated elements of pop, [[Jazz|jazz]], rock and other genres. She began singing in nightclubs in [[Saskatoon]] and [[Toronto]] before moving to the United States in 1965. Her debut album, *Song to a Seagull* (1968), was followed by *Blue* (1971), often cited as one of the greatest albums of all time. [[Rolling Stone]] ranked *Blue* 30th in its 2003 list of the "500 Greatest Albums of All Time" and placed it at number 3 in its 2020 edition. Her jazz-influenced *Court and Spark* (1974) was her best-selling album. She won eleven [[Grammy Awards]], was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1997, and received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2002.

Hashemite kingdom in the Southern [[Levant]] region of West Asia. It is bordered by [[Syria]] to the north, Iraq to the east, [[Saudi Arabia]] to the south, and [[Israel]] and the West Bank to the west. Its capital and largest city is [[Amman]], and the country covers 89,342 sq km (34,495 sq mi) with a population of 11.5 million. It is a semi-constitutional monarchy in which the king holds wide executive and legislative powers. Transjordan became a British protectorate in 1921, and the country gained independence in 1946. It is a founding member of the [[Arab League]]. Around 95% of the population is [[Islam|Sunni Muslim]], and in 2015 about 2.1 million Palestinian refugees, most with Jordanian citizenship, and 1.4 million Syrian refugees lived in the country. It ranks 100th on the [[Human Development Index]].

American former stockbroker and businessman. He pleaded guilty in 1999 to fraud linked to a penny-stock scheme run from a boiler room, and served 22 months in prison after becoming an FBI informant. By his account, he had been laid off as a trainee stockbroker after the [[Black Monday (1987)|Black Monday]] crash of 1987. His memoir *The Wolf of Wall Street* (2007) was adapted into a 2013 film by [[Martin Scorsese]], in which [[Leonardo DiCaprio]] played him.

Canadian psychologist, author and media commentator. He resigned from the [[University of Toronto]] in 2021. His 2016 [[YouTube]] videos opposed Bill C-16, a proposed federal law banning discrimination based on gender identity and expression; it became law in 2017. His second book, *12 Rules for Life: An Antidote to Chaos* (2018), became an international bestseller. He has been criticized by climate scientists for denying the scientific consensus on [[Climate change|climate change]]. In 2022 he became chancellor of Ralston College in [[Savannah, Georgia]]. In 2025 he was hospitalized for five months with chronic inflammatory response syndrome.

River in the [[Levant]], draining to the [[Dead Sea]]. The 251 km (156 mi) endorheic river flows roughly north to south through the Sea of Galilee. [[Jordan]] and the [[Golan Heights]] border it to the east, while Israel and the West Bank lie to the west. Its name may derive from a Semitic word meaning "flow down"; the earliest known use appears in an Egyptian papyrus probably from the reign of Rameses II. The river holds major significance in Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The [[Bible]] describes the [[Israelites]] crossing it into the Promised Land, and [[Jesus]] being baptized in it by [[John the Baptist]]. Upstream diversions and dams have greatly reduced its flow.

Brazilian novelist of the modernist school. Amado is the best-known modern Brazilian writer, with works translated into some 49 languages and popularized in film, including *Dona Flor and Her Two Husbands* (1976). He was nominated for the [[Nobel Prize]] in Literature at least seven times. Amado knew the misery of workers on the cocoa plantations near his birthplace in Itabuna, in [[Bahia]], a theme in *The Violent Land* (1944). A Communist militant, he was elected to the National Constituent Assembly in 1945 and spent periods in exile in [[Argentina]] and [[Uruguay]]. He occupied the 23rd chair of the Brazilian Academy of Letters from 1961 until his death.

Argentine short-story writer, essayist, poet and translator. Born in [[Buenos Aires]], he moved with his family to Switzerland in 1914 and studied at the *Collège de Genève*. On his return to Argentina in 1921 he began publishing poems and essays in surrealist journals and worked as a librarian. His best-known collections, *Ficciones* and *El Aleph*, published in the 1940s, explore labyrinths, infinity, mirrors, dreams and fictional writers. His work influenced the [[Fantasy|fantasy]] genre and the magical realist movement in [[Latin American literature]]. In 1955 he was appointed director of the National Public Library, and he was completely blind by the age of 55. In 1961 he shared the first International Formentor Prize with [[Samuel Beckett]]. His final work, *The Conspirators*, was dedicated to [[Geneva]].

Angolan politician and military officer. He served as the second president of Angola from 1979 to 2017, and as commander-in-chief of the armed forces and leader of the MPLA. He joined the MPLA while still at school and studied petroleum engineering and radar communications in the [[Soviet Union]]. He served as foreign minister under [[Agostinho Neto]] and became president after Neto's death in 1979, with Soviet support. In 1991 his government agreed to a multi-party system, and the MPLA moved from communism to [[Social democracy|social democracy]]. He was elected in 1992 over UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi, and in 1997 he contributed to a rebel invasion of [[Zaire]] that overthrew [[Mobutu Sese Seko]]. He retired in 2017, succeeded by João Lourenço. He was criticized as a dictator and accused of creating one of the most corrupt regimes in Africa.

Cuban nationalist, poet, essayist and national hero. Born in [[Havana]] under Spanish rule, he began political activism at an early age and traveled widely in [[Spain]], Latin America and the United States to promote Cuban independence. He designed the ideology of the Cuban Revolutionary Party and unified the Cuban émigré community, particularly in [[Florida]]. He founded newspapers, including *Patria*, which was an important instrument in his campaign for independence. He died in military action during the Battle of Dos Ríos. Many of his verses from *Versos Sencillos* were later adapted into the song "Guantanamera," which became a prominent song of [[Cuba]]. His writings influenced the [[Nicaragua|Nicaraguan]] poet Rubén Darío, and after the [[Cuban Revolution]] his ideology became a major motif in Cuban politics.

Portuguese football manager. A former midfielder, he has managed clubs including [[Inter Milan]], Chelsea and Real Madrid. He has won league titles in four countries and is one of only seven managers to have won the [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] with two clubs. He is the only manager to have won all three current [[UEFA]] club competitions. He won a treble with Inter Milan in 2010 and was named the inaugural [[FIFA]] World Coach of the Year. Nicknamed "The Special One," he drew comparisons with Helenio Herrera.

Filipino nationalist, writer and [[Polymath|polymath]]. An [[Ophthalmology|ophthalmologist]] by training, he became a key writer of the Propaganda Movement, which advocated political reforms for the colony under Spain. Growing more separatist in the early 1890s, he founded the secret society La Liga Filipina in [[Manila]] in 1892 and was arrested that July, then banished to [[Mindanao]]. In exile he met Josephine Bracken, who became his common-law wife. He left for [[Cuba]] in 1896 but was arrested in [[Barcelona]] after the [[Philippine Revolution]] broke out, and was executed for rebellion. He approved of the revolution's goals but was not involved in planning it. His novels *Noli Me Tángere* (1887) and *El filibusterismo* (1891) are taken together as a national epic, and though he is widely considered a national hero, no law has officially proclaimed him one.

Portuguese writer. He received the 1998 Nobel Prize in Literature for parables sustained by imagination, compassion and irony. His allegorical works often present subversive perspectives on historic events, and he was an atheist and a proponent of libertarian [[Communism|communism]]. He criticized the [[Catholic Church]], the [[European Union]] and the [[International Monetary Fund]], and defended love as a means to improve the human condition. In 1992 the Portuguese government ordered his novel *The Gospel According to Jesus Christ* removed from the Aristeion Prize shortlist as religiously offensive, and he went into exile on Lanzarote, Spain. In 2007 he founded the José Saramago Foundation to promote the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]].

Argentine general and independence leader. Born in Yapeyú, Corrientes, he went to study in [[Málaga]], [[Spain]], at the age of seven and later fought in the [[Peninsular War]] against France. In 1812 he sailed to [[Buenos Aires]] and offered his services to the independence cause. Leading the Army of the Andes, he crossed the Andes into [[Chile]] and won the battles of Chacabuco and Maipú, liberating Chile from royalist rule. After seizing partial control of [[Lima]], he was appointed Protector of Peru in 1821, when Peruvian independence was declared. In 1822 he met [[Simón Bolívar]] at [[Guayaquil]], then resigned his command and moved to France in 1824. He is regarded as a national hero of Argentina, Chile and Peru, and the Order of the Liberator General San Martín is Argentina's highest decoration.

Empress of the French, first wife of [[Napoleon]]. Her first husband, Alexandre de Beauharnais, was [[Guillotine|guillotined]] during the [[Reign of Terror]], and she was imprisoned until five days after his execution. Her marriage to Napoleon was annulled in 1810 because she had borne him no children. Through her children by Beauharnais, she was the grandmother of [[Napoleon III]]. She was also Queen of Italy from 1805 until the annulment. A patron of the arts, she shaped the Consular and [[Empire style|empire style]] at the Château de Malmaison, which was noted for its rose garden.

German military officer and physician. Known as the "Angel of Death," he conducted experiments on prisoners at Auschwitz II-Birkenau, where he helped select victims for the gas chambers during [[The Holocaust|the Holocaust]]. He joined the [[Nazi Party]] in 1937 and the [[Schutzstaffel|SS]] in 1938. After the war he fled to Argentina and later lived in [[Paraguay]] and Brazil, sought by West Germany, Israel and Nazi hunters, but was never caught. He drowned after a [[Stroke|stroke]] while swimming off the coast of Bertioga and was buried under a false name.

Dynastic kingdom of [[Korea]], 1392–1897. Founded by [[Taejo of Joseon|Taejo]] after the overthrow of [[Goryeo]], it moved the capital to modern-day [[Seoul]] in 1393. It made [[Confucianism|Neo-Confucianism]] the state ideology and discouraged [[Buddhism]]. The period saw the height of classical Korean culture, trade, literature, science and technology. Failed Japanese invasions in 1592 and 1598 and later invasions from [[Manchuria]] in 1627 and by the [[Qing dynasty]] in 1636–1637 severely weakened the kingdom. The kingdom pursued an increasingly harsh isolationist policy, earning the name "hermit kingdom" in Western literature, and declined in the late 19th century. Modern Korean bureaucracy and administrative divisions were established during the period, and the modern Korean language derives from its traditions.

English naturalist, botanist and patron of the natural sciences. He first made his name on a 1766 natural-history expedition to [[Newfoundland and Labrador]]. He then joined [[James Cook|Captain James Cook]]'s first great voyage (1768–1771), visiting Brazil, Tahiti, New Zealand and Australia. As president of the Royal Society for over 41 years, he advised [[George III|King George III]] on the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew, which he made the world's leading botanical garden. He is credited with bringing 30,000 plant specimens home and with introducing [[Eucalyptus|eucalyptus]], acacia and the genus *Banksia* to the [[Western world]]. He advocated British settlement in [[New South Wales]] and the use of Botany Bay for convicts.
